3.1 Research design and data
   I measure currency-level FX risk using the ICRG‟s exchange
rate    stability         risk       ratings.         The      ICRG       dataset     provides
measures of political, economic, and financial risk ratings
that have been widely used in prior studies. 11 The dataset
covers more than 140 countries and assigns an exchange rate
stability     risk       point       for     each       country        for     a   given       year
( 𝐹𝑋𝑆𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒 ). The risk points range from 0 to 10, with a higher
value representing a more stable currency.12 To measure FX risk
at the firm level, I develop a continuous measure, 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 , by
weighting     𝐹𝑋𝑆𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒       by       the    number       of     affiliates          located      in
jurisdictions        using       a    particular          currency         relative       to    the
total number of foreign subsidiaries:
                                                     # 𝑜𝑓 𝑎𝑓𝑓𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠 𝑢𝑠𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑐𝑖,𝑡
              𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘𝑖,𝑡 = − ∑ 𝐹𝑋𝑆𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒𝑐,𝑡 ∗
                                                          # 𝑜𝑓 𝑎𝑓𝑓𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑖,𝑡
where    c,    i,       and      t     denote        currency,           firm,      and     year,
respectively.13 I reverse the sign of 𝐹𝑋𝑆𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑒 in the calculation
above so that 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 increases in exchange rate volatility.
Information related to the location of foreign affiliates is
disclosed     in     Exhibit         21     of    10-K       reports;         I    obtain      such

11
     Examples include Beck, Demirgüç-Kunt, and Levine [2003]; Claessens and
Laeven [2003]; Bekaert, Harvey, and Lundblad [2005]; Gelos and Wei [2005];
and Cannizzaro and Weiner [2015].
  12
     For instance, a currency with an annual appreciation of less than 9.9%
or a depreciation of less than 4.9% is assigned a risk point of 10, whereas
a currency with an annual appreciation of 10-14.9% or a depreciation of 5-
7.4% is assigned a risk point of 9.5. For a few countries that are not
covered by the ICRG and use currencies pegged to the dollar, I assume a
risk point of 10 for years when the currency peg is effective.
  13
     While it is possible to construct a continuous measure of FX risk
exposure based on changes in the cumulative translation adjustment account
at the firm level, such a measure is problematic because (1) translation
gains and losses are netted so changes in the account may understate the
volatile nature of foreign currencies, and (2) the measure can be driven by
one or two extremely volatile currencies that are not representative of the
currencies in which foreign affiliates primarily generate and expend cash.

disclosures from the EX-21 Dataset provided by Scott Dyreng,
who first used the data in Dyreng and Lindsey [2009].14
     To estimate income shifting, I adopt the approach developed
by Collins et al. [1998] and use the multiperiod measures
suggested by Klassen and Laplante [2012b]. The Collins et al.
[1998] approach captures income shifting through both transfer
pricing and investment location decisions. Motivated by Dyreng
and Markle [2016], I add several firm-level control variables
to     the    baseline       model        that      are      likely         correlated   with
accounting profitability and tax incentives. To test H1, I
examine how the tax-motivated income shifting intensity varies
based on FX risk:

     𝐹𝑅𝑂𝑆𝑖,𝑡 = 𝛽0 + 𝛽1 𝐹𝑇𝑅𝑖,𝑡 + 𝛽2 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘𝑖,𝑡−4 + 𝛽3 𝐹𝑇𝑅 ∗ 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 + 𝛴𝛽4𝑛 𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑜𝑙𝑠 +
               𝛴𝛽5𝑘 𝐼𝑁𝐷𝑖,𝑡 + 𝛴𝛽6𝑡 𝑌𝐸𝐴𝑅𝑖,𝑡 + 𝜀𝑖,𝑡,
                               (1)

where:
 𝐹𝑅𝑂𝑆𝑖,𝑡     = Sum of foreign pretax income (t-4 to t) / sum of
               foreign sales (t-4 to t);
 𝐹𝑇𝑅𝑖,𝑡      = Sum of foreign taxes (t-4 to t) / sum of foreign
               pretax income (t-4 to t) - sum of U.S. statutory tax
               rates (t-4 to t) / 5;

 𝐼𝑁𝐷𝑖,𝑡      = A vector of industry indicator variables; and
 𝑌𝐸𝐴𝑅𝑖,𝑡     = A vector of year indicator variables.


     In Equation (1), 𝐹𝑇𝑅 captures a firm‟s long-run incentive to
shift income. For simplicity, firm-years with a negative 𝐹𝑇𝑅
value are referred to as “potential outbound income shifters”

throughout      this       study.         To      ease       the       interpretation               of
coefficients,        I    demean       both      𝐹𝑇𝑅      and     𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘          when       the   two
variables interact. Therefore, the coefficient on 𝐹𝑇𝑅 measures
the    extent   of       tax-motivated          income       shifting         for        U.S.      MNCs
experiencing average FX risk and is expected to be negative.
All    financial      variables         in     the     equation         are       available         in
COMPUSTAT. I measure 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 at year t-4 to examine how currency
volatility      affects          a      firm‟s         long-run           income          shifting
activities. According to H1, I predict a positive coefficient
on 𝐹𝑇𝑅 ∗ 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 for the potential outbound income shifters.

3.2 Sample selection and descriptive statistics
  My sample selection criteria are described in Table 1, Panel
A. I begin with the sample of all profitable firm-years with
non-missing multiperiod measures (i.e., 𝐹𝑅𝑂𝑆 , 𝐹𝑇𝑅 , and 𝑅𝑂𝑆 )
available in COMPUSTAT. Consistent with prior studies in the

income shifting literature, I exclude financial institutions
(SIC codes 6000–6999), utilities (SIC codes 4900–4999), and
non-U.S. firms. To construct the sample of firms with tax
incentives to shift income outbound, I require firms to have
𝐹𝑇𝑅 values less than zero. 17 I further drop firms with missing
CIK numbers, which are needed for merging the COMPUSTAT data
with    the   EX-21    Dataset         and     the      hand-collected            derivative
hedging data. To ensure consistent income tax reporting, the
sample    period      begins      with       1993     because         the       Statement    of
Financial Accounting Standards 109 became effective for fiscal
years beginning after December 15, 1992. I end my sample in
2017, which is the year before the TCJA was adopted. 18 After
merging with the EX-21 Dataset, the final sample for tests
involving 𝐹𝑋𝑅𝑖𝑠𝑘 contains 5,432 firm-year observations, or 980
unique    firms.       Since      the       financial           derivative            indicator
variable requires only non-missing 10-K reports, the final
sample for financial derivative tests is slightly larger and
contains 6,271 firm-year observations, or 1,082 unique firms.

17
     This means that the main sample does not include potential inbound
income shifters. I explore whether FX volatility has an impact on inbound
income shifting in Section 5.3.
  18
     This means that variables measured at t-4 cover the period 1993 – 2013,
whereas variables measured from t-4 to t cover the period 1997 – 2017.
